name: JRC Global Surface Water and its monthly history

identity.method_name: JRC Global Surface Water (GSW) Mapping Layers, including Monthly History and Yearly History, v1.4 (current Earth Engine catalog release as of 2026)
identity.core_idea: The European Commission Joint Research Centre (JRC), with Google, ran an expert-system (decision-tree plus evidential-reasoning) classifier over every usable Landsat 5/7/8 scene since 1984 (4,716,475 scenes as of v1.4) to label each 30 m pixel as water or non-water on every available date. These per-scene classifications are then aggregated into monthly and yearly water-history image collections, and further summarised into occurrence, seasonality, recurrence, change-intensity and transition-class layers that describe how often, when, and how consistently each pixel has held water since 1984. It is the standard global reference product for long-term surface-water dynamics, independent of any single project's own index or sensor.
identity.official_dataset_ids: JRC/GSW1_4/GlobalSurfaceWater (summary statistics layers: occurrence, change_abs, change_norm, seasonality, recurrence, transition, max_extent); JRC/GSW1_4/MonthlyHistory (per-month water/not-water/no-data classification, 454 monthly images, 1984-03 to 2021-12); JRC/GSW1_4/YearlyHistory (per-year waterClass: 0 no data, 1 not water, 2 seasonal water, 3 permanent water, 1984-2021); JRC/GSW1_4/MonthlyRecurrence; JRC/GSW1_4/Metadata. Current version as of 2026 in the Google Earth Engine Data Catalog is v1.4 (namespace JRC/GSW1_4/...), covering 16 March 1984 to 31 December 2021 [verify -- confirmed directly from the Earth Engine catalog pages for GlobalSurfaceWater, MonthlyHistory and YearlyHistory on 2026-09-17]. The JRC's own Global Surface Water Explorer portal (global-surface-water.appspot.com) separately advertises a newer v1.5 product extending to 1984-2024 (Landsat Collection 1 for 1984-2021, Landsat Collection 2 thereafter), available for direct download/FTP from JRC, but as of this check v1.5 was NOT yet mirrored into the standard Earth Engine JRC/ namespace (no JRC_GSW1_5_GlobalSurfaceWater catalog page found; only scattered references to project-level assets such as GSW1_5/YearlyHistory_2016_2021 and GSW1_5/YearlyHistory_2022_2024) [uncertain -- GEE availability of v1.5 could not be fully confirmed and should be re-checked in the Earth Engine catalog directly before relying on it].

fit_to_project.ground_truth_proxy_strategy: Data-source used as an independent cross-check layer, not a label-generation strategy in itself. GSW does not supply encroachment labels; it supplies an independently-derived water/non-water and water-history record against which the project's own MNDWI>0-derived water_ha figures can be compared for agreement or divergence, scene by scene and year by year. The correct framing for this project is: GSW is evidence used to validate or flag the project's own outcome variable, not a substitute training signal, and it costs nothing beyond Earth Engine API calls and a few days of comparison analysis.
fit_to_project.input_required: Only the lake polygon (the existing OpenStreetMap multipolygon) and a target date or year; GSW is queried directly from Earth Engine (ee.Image('JRC/GSW1_4/GlobalSurfaceWater') or ee.ImageCollection('JRC/GSW1_4/YearlyHistory')) and reduced over the polygon. Nothing new needs to be acquired beyond what the project already has (an Earth Engine account/service key, which the project presumably already uses for Sentinel-2 access via Earth Search/AWS, or a separate GEE account for this dataset only since GSW is GEE/JRC-hosted, not on AWS Earth Search).
fit_to_project.viable_with_42_rows: yes-if-reframed. GSW comparison naturally produces one water-area (or occurrence/seasonality) value per lake per year, i.e. up to 42 additional rows/columns that align one-to-one with the project's existing lake-year table -- this is the one dataset in this item pair that slots directly into the 42-row structure without needing a pixel-level reframing argument. However, because GSW's Yearly History for 2019-2021 only overlaps 3 of the project's 7 years (see resolution/coverage below), the usable cross-check sample is at most 6 lakes x 3 years = 18 rows, not 42.
fit_to_project.viable_without_ground_truth: yes, and this is the point of the item. GSW is itself an independent, non-project-derived estimate of water extent, so it does not need the project's ground truth; it substitutes an external reference for the missing ground truth, at least for the years it covers. It cannot validate the water label in 2022-2025 because JRC v1.4 does not extend there (see below).
fit_to_project.resolution_match_20m: Mismatch, and it must be stated plainly: GSW is native 30 m Landsat, the project's grid is a resampled 20 m Sentinel-2 EPSG:32643 grid. This is not a resampling-preserves-everything situation -- a 30 m Landsat pixel footprint does not align with a 20 m Sentinel-2 pixel, so any per-pixel comparison requires reprojecting one onto the other (recommended: reduce both to total hectares within the lake polygon via zonal statistics, not pixel-to-pixel comparison, to avoid resampling artefacts). For a 6-lake, small-to-medium urban lake study, several lakes may only be tens of Landsat pixels across, so 30 m GSW carries meaningfully coarser shoreline detail than the project's own 20 m mask, especially for narrow or irregularly shaped lake margins.
fit_to_project.label_source_needed: None required from the project; GSW is itself the independent label/reference source being proposed. No supervision needed to use it.
fit_to_project.fixes_which_stated_limitation: Directly addresses limitation (3), no real ground truth -- GSW is external, non-circular evidence against which the project's own MNDWI threshold can be checked for at least a 3-year overlap window (2019-2021). It does not address limitation (1) (42 rows; if anything it can only ever contribute a subset of those rows given the coverage gap), does not address limitation (2) (OpenStreetMap buildings), and does not directly address limitation (4) (one dry-season scene per year) except that GSW's own monthly history could, in principle, be used to characterise the seasonal water cycle the project's single annual scene misses -- but only for 2019-2021.
fit_to_project.handles_desilting_confound: Partially, and this is GSW's most useful contribution to the project. The 'seasonality' layer (months of the year with water, per pixel, per year) and 'recurrence' layer (percentage of years since 1984 that water returned to a given pixel) can distinguish a location that is seasonally dry within a year (i.e. genuinely part of the lake's normal wet/dry cycle, high multi-decadal recurrence but low seasonality in a given year) from one that has been intentionally, unusually drained (a location with high historical recurrence -- e.g. >90% of the 1984-2021 record -- that suddenly shows near-zero occurrence for one specific year, such as Bellandur's 2021 desilting low of 0.4 ha) versus one that is genuinely and durably lost to encroachment (a location with declining recurrence trending toward zero across multiple consecutive years, not a single-year dip). This gives an evidence-based way to argue 'this drop is a known desilting event, not encroachment' using an external, non-project dataset, but only for the years GSW covers (see below), so it cannot evaluate the 2025 Bellandur value (107.9 ha) at all against this reference.
fit_to_project.handles_hyacinth_confound: No, and this is the central independence caveat for this item. GSW's expert-system classifier is itself an optical, Landsat-spectral-index-driven water detector (it uses Landsat-band spectral tests, not radar or a hyacinth-specific spectral signature), so a hyacinth mat -- which is emergent/floating vegetation with a vegetation-like spectral signature, not open water -- will very likely also be classified as 'not water' by GSW's expert system, exactly as the project's own NDVI-based vegetation mask would classify it. This means GSW independently CONFIRMS a mat is not open water (useful for cross-checking the water side of the ledger) but does NOT independently resolve whether that non-water area is a hyacinth mat, bare lakebed, or actual encroachment -- GSW has no vegetation-type discrimination at all. For the hyacinth confound specifically, GSW's yearly water class for Bellandur/Varthur would likely show a large 'not water' area during hyacinth bloom years that is indistinguishable, in GSW alone, from encroachment, bare soil, or a dry lakebed. The Bellandur/Varthur macrophyte-cover paper (MDPI Remote Sensing 2020, doi 10.3390/rs12223843) remains the correct external cross-check for hyacinth specifically; GSW does not substitute for it.
fit_to_project.legal_traceability: None. GSW is a physical water-occurrence product with no reference to any cadastral, legal or administrative boundary; it does not know about the Bengaluru Master Plan 30 m buffer, the earlier 75 m NGT buffer, Karnataka Tank Conservation and Development Authority records, Survey of India records, Bhuvan, or the National Wetland Atlas 2024. Using it changes nothing about the legal standing of the OpenStreetMap lake polygon the project already uses; it only strengthens (or weakens) confidence in the physical water-extent number computed inside that same non-statutory polygon.
fit_to_project.temporal_granularity: Genuinely varies year to year and even month to month within the years it covers (1984-2021 for Yearly/Monthly History) -- this is real, independently-observed temporal signal, not a static snapshot. But the critical caveat for this specific project is that GSW v1.4's coverage (1984-2021) overlaps only 3 of the project's 7 target years (2019, 2020, 2021) and stops BEFORE 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025 -- so for more than half of the project's study window (4 of 7 years, including the most recent, most policy-relevant years) GSW provides zero temporal signal at all under the version actually available in Earth Engine as of 2026.

implementation.libraries: Google Earth Engine Python API (earthengine-api) or JavaScript Code Editor; geemap or ee for zonal reduction over the lake polygon; no local heavy compute needed since GSW is queried as a pre-computed image collection server-side on Google's infrastructure.
implementation.pretrained_weights: Not applicable in the ML sense -- GSW is a pre-computed, already-classified raster product, not a model the project runs. There is no model to download or fine-tune; the 'model' (JRC's expert-system classifier) has already been applied by JRC to produce the published layers.
implementation.licence: Free and open. JRC Global Surface Water data are released for unrestricted use with attribution ('Source: EC JRC/Google'), consistent with the Copernicus/JRC open-data policy; accessible via Google Earth Engine at no cost within normal Earth Engine non-commercial/academic usage limits, and via direct FTP download from the JRC Global Surface Water Explorer portal.
implementation.compute_requirement: Trivial. Zonal statistics (mean occurrence, area-weighted water class counts) over 6 small lake polygons for a handful of years is a lightweight Earth Engine reduceRegion call that runs in seconds; no GPU, no local heavy compute, fully reproducible on a laptop with an internet connection and a free Earth Engine account.
implementation.student_days: 0.5-1.5 student-days: setting up Earth Engine access (if not already used for Sentinel-2 retrieval; note GSW is GEE-native, the project's Sentinel-2 pipeline is Earth Search/AWS-native, so this may be the first GEE touchpoint and could add setup time if the student has not used GEE before), writing the zonal-reduction script for occurrence/seasonality/recurrence/transition per lake per available year, and producing a short comparison table/plot of GSW water hectares vs the project's MNDWI water_ha for 2019-2021.

evaluation.metrics: Simple agreement/divergence metrics between GSW-derived water hectares (per lake, per overlapping year) and the project's own MNDWI-derived water_ha: absolute and percentage difference, and a qualitative flag ('confound-consistent' vs 'discrepant') driven by the recurrence/seasonality layers. This is a cross-validation exercise, not a model to be scored by precision/recall in the usual sense, since GSW itself is not a perfect ground truth, only an independent second opinion.
evaluation.validation_protocol: Not a train/test split problem -- GSW is used as an external check, applied identically across all 6 lakes for the 3 overlapping years (2019-2021), so there is no leakage risk from data splitting. The correct presentation is leave-nothing-out: report the GSW-vs-project comparison for every lake-year where both exist, and explicitly report the years where GSW provides no comparison (2022-2025) as a stated coverage gap rather than silently omitting them.
evaluation.leakage_risk: Low for the comparison itself, since GSW is generated entirely independently of the project's own Sentinel-2 pipeline (different sensor, different processing chain, different institution). The one leakage-adjacent risk is over-interpretation: if a panel is shown 'GSW agrees with our threshold' only for the 3 years where GSW is available, and the remaining 4 years (including the years with the most interesting desilting/hyacinth dynamics) are quietly left unchecked, the comparison could be presented as stronger validation of the whole 2019-2025 series than it actually is. This must be disclosed explicitly.
evaluation.uncertainty_reporting: GSW itself reports validated overall Landsat-scene classification accuracy from JRC's own control-point validation (40,124 control points globally) [verify -- aggregate accuracy figure by class was not independently re-derived from the primary validation report in this pass and should be quoted directly from Pekel et al. 2016 Extended Data or the JRC technical documentation before being cited numerically], but this is a global figure, not a Bengaluru-specific or Bellandur/Varthur-specific accuracy estimate, and JRC does not provide a lake-specific or per-pixel credible interval. The project should report the GSW-vs-project comparison as a point-estimate cross-check with the explicit caveat that GSW's own accuracy is unvalidated locally, not as a calibrated probability.
evaluation.augmentation_honesty_risk: Not applicable -- GSW is used as a fixed, external reference layer, not as a source of synthetic or augmented training data.

evidence.published_performance: JRC Global Surface Water global validation used 40,124 independently distributed control points and reports high overall water/non-water classification accuracy [verify -- exact percentage figures (commonly cited as >97-99% error rates being <1-3% in various summaries) should be quoted directly from Pekel et al. 2016 main text/Extended Data Table before being used numerically in the project write-up, as this pass could not fully re-derive the exact published number from a primary source]. Between 1984 and 2015 the paper reports permanent water loss of almost 90,000 km2 globally and gain elsewhere, illustrating the product's designed purpose (multi-decadal global change detection), not fine-scale accuracy for individual small urban lakes.
evidence.study_area_of_that_work: Global -- more than 3 million Landsat scenes across the whole planet, 1984-2015 (extended to 2021 in v1.4 and reportedly to 2024 in the JRC portal's v1.5). This is emphatically not a study of Bengaluru or of any of the 6 project lakes specifically; the global validation point density in and around small Indian urban lakes is almost certainly far lower than in the well-sampled regions used for the headline validation statistics, so the published global accuracy figure should not be assumed to transfer directly to Bellandur, Varthur or the other 4 lakes without local sanity-checking.
evidence.applies_to_indian_urban_lakes: No dedicated Bengaluru or Bellandur/Varthur validation of GSW was found in this pass [verify]. GSW has been used in numerous India-wide and South-Asia-wide surface water studies as a reference layer (e.g. Pune-district Landsat water-mapping literature found during this research references GSW-style products generally), but no paper specifically validating GSW's accuracy against ground truth for Bengaluru's small urban lakes, or for Bellandur/Varthur's hyacinth-affected waters specifically, was located.
evidence.evidence_recency: 2016 for the foundational Pekel et al. Nature paper describing the method and v1.0-era validation; 2021 (v1.4, current Earth Engine catalog release) for the most recent officially catalogued temporal extent; 2024 [uncertain] for the JRC portal's own v1.5 extension, which was not confirmed as available through Earth Engine as of this check.
evidence.primary_sources: Pekel, J.-F., Cottam, A., Gorelick, N., Belward, A.S. (2016). 'High-resolution mapping of global surface water and its long-term changes.' Nature 540, 418-422. https://doi.org/10.1038/nature20584 ; JRC Global Surface Water Mapping Layers, v1.4, Earth Engine Data Catalog: https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/catalog/JRC_GSW1_4_GlobalSurfaceWater ; JRC Monthly Water History, v1.4: https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/catalog/JRC_GSW1_4_MonthlyHistory ; JRC Yearly Water Classification History, v1.4: https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/catalog/JRC_GSW1_4_YearlyHistory ; Global Surface Water Explorer (JRC portal, v1.5 announcement, 1984-2024): https://global-surface-water.appspot.com/download ; JRC Data Catalogue collection page: https://data.jrc.ec.europa.eu/collection/id-0084 [verify -- fetch of this specific page failed during this research pass with a connection error and should be retried].

risk.failure_modes: (1) Coverage gap: GSW v1.4 (the version actually in Earth Engine as of 2026) ends 31 December 2021, so it can cross-check only 2019-2021 of the project's 2019-2025 window -- 4 of 7 years, including the 2022-2025 period that contains the most dramatic Bellandur desilting recovery (0.4 ha in 2021 to 107.9 ha in 2025), get zero independent water-extent check from this dataset unless the unconfirmed v1.5 becomes available in Earth Engine. (2) Resolution mismatch: 30 m Landsat vs 20 m Sentinel-2 means shoreline-level disagreement is expected even where both datasets are 'correct' by their own definitions, purely from pixel-footprint differences, especially on narrow or irregular lake margins. (3) Shared blind spot: because GSW is also an optical, spectral-index-based water/non-water classifier, it will very likely mislabel hyacinth mats as 'not water' in the same direction as the project's own NDVI-based mask -- so a naive 'GSW agrees with us' result on a hyacinth-affected lake-year would look like independent confirmation but could actually be two different sensors making the same underlying category error against the true land cover (open water hidden under vegetation). (4) A panel could reasonably ask why v1.5 (extending to 2024) was not used if it is real and downloadable -- the student should proactively resolve whether v1.5 is usable (direct download and reprocessing outside Earth Engine, or wait for Earth Engine mirroring) rather than silently using the older, shorter-coverage version.
risk.panel_defensibility: GSW survives the 'is this really independent' question better than another optical index run on the same Sentinel-2 imagery would, because it is a different sensor (Landsat vs Sentinel-2), a different institution (JRC/Google vs the project), a different algorithm (expert-system decision tree over decades of scenes vs a single-date MNDWI threshold), and a different processing chain end to end. But the student must be honest that GSW and the project's MNDWI mask are still both optical, passive, visible/near-infrared/SWIR-based water detectors, so they share the fundamental limitation of being fooled by anything that is spectrally non-water-like but hydrologically water-covered (hyacinth mats, dense algal bloom, turbid or vegetated shallows). A panel asking 'so GSW isn't really independent, it's just another spectral index' should be answered: independent of the project's specific implementation and sensor, yes; independent of the underlying physical principle (reflectance-based optical water detection), no -- true sensor-type independence would require radar (e.g. Sentinel-1 SAR) or field survey, neither of which this item provides.
risk.honest_expectation: A realistic, reportable outcome is: 'For 2019-2021, our MNDWI-derived water_ha for [lake] agrees/disagrees with JRC GSW's independently-derived water extent within X%, and GSW's seasonality/recurrence layers are consistent/inconsistent with a desilting explanation for the observed dip.' For 2022-2025, GSW (v1.4) provides no comparison at all, and this must be stated as a clean coverage gap rather than papered over. A null or partial-coverage result -- 'independent validation is only possible for 3 of our 7 years, and even then only confirms the water/non-water boundary, not the hyacinth-vs-water distinction' -- is the honest and expected finding, not a failure of the analysis.

verdict.recommended_rank: adopt-if-time -- genuinely useful as a free, low-effort, structurally independent (different sensor, different institution, different algorithm) cross-check on the project's own water mask for 2019-2021, and its seasonality/recurrence layers are the single best available external evidence for arguing a given water-area dip is desilting rather than encroachment, but its coverage stops before 2022 (v1.4, the version confirmed in Earth Engine) and it shares the same optical-spectral blind spot to hyacinth as the project's own method, so it cannot resolve the project's other central confound.
verdict.one_line_for_the_guide: We cross-checked our 2019-2021 water-area figures against the independent, Landsat-derived JRC Global Surface Water dataset (different sensor and algorithm from our own Sentinel-2 MNDWI threshold), used its seasonality and recurrence layers to help argue that some water-area dips are desilting rather than encroachment, but could not extend this check to 2022-2025 because that version of the dataset ends in 2021, and it still cannot separate open water from water hyacinth because it is also a spectral, optical classifier.
